t: Inheritance, polymorphism, evaluating OOP and event-driven programming
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson AP25: Inheritance, polymorphism, evaluating OOP and event-driven programming.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Explain inheritance and work out which attributes and methods a subclass object has. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Once a programmer can write classes and create objects, the next step is to make classes work together. Inheritance allows a new class to be built from an existing one, so a sports club system can define a general Member class once and then derive Junior and Adult classes that inherit everything a member has while adding their own details. Polymorphism builds on inheritance: the same method call, such as Fee, can produce different results depending on which kind of object receives it, so a single loop can process a mixed list of members without checking each one's type. Together with encapsulation, these are the features that make object-oriented programming powerful for large systems.
Makes sense. Keep going.

However, OOP is not automatically the best choice, so programmers must be able to evaluate it, weighing benefits such as realistic modelling, code reuse and reduced testing against extra complexity and a poor fit for some problems. Finally, this lesson looks at event-driven programming, in which the order of execution is decided by events such as button clicks. Graphical user interfaces are the most familiar example, and their buttons, text boxes and labels are themselves objects.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Inheritance is the mechanism by which a new, more specialised class takes on the attributes and methods of an existing, more general class. The general class is called the superclass, base class or parent class, and the specialised class is the subclass, derived class or child class. In C sharp the relationship is written with a colon, as in class Junior: Member. A subclass automatically has every attribute and method of its superclass and normally adds members of its own, so attributes accumulate as you move down a class hierarchy: if Member has two attributes and Junior adds one, a Junior object holds three. A subclass does not have to add anything, but usually does.
Got it. Keep going.

Subclasses are independent of each other, so a method defined only in Junior cannot be used on an Adult object. Inheritance models an 'is a' relationship: a junior is a member, and a bus is a vehicle. If that sentence sounds wrong, inheritance is probably the wrong design. Hierarchies can have several levels, and a class hierarchy diagram shows the superclass at the top with lines and hollow arrowheads pointing up to it from each subclass.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

A subclass has its own constructor, but the superclass's attributes still need to be initialised. In C sharp the subclass constructor passes values up to the superclass constructor using: base(...), for example public Junior(int no, string n, string phone): base(no, n), and then sets its own new attributes in its body. Private attributes of the superclass are inherited in the sense that every subclass object contains them, but code written in the subclass cannot refer to them directly; it must use the superclass's public get and set methods. Declaring a member protected, shown by # in a class diagram, makes it accessible inside the superclass and its subclasses while keeping it hidden from all other code.
Okay. Keep going.

Sometimes a superclass describes an idea so general that no object should ever be created from it directly, such as Account in a credit union system where every account is in fact either a SavingsAccount or a LoanAccount. Declaring the class abstract prevents instantiation, so new Account(...) will not compile. An abstract class may contain abstract methods, which have a header but no body, and each non-abstract subclass is then forced to provide its own overriding version.
Go on.

Polymorphism, from the Greek for 'many forms', is the ability of objects of different classes to respond to the same method call in their own way. In C sharp it is achieved by overriding. The base class declares a method as virtual, meaning subclasses are allowed to replace it, or as abstract, meaning they must. A subclass then supplies a method with the same name, parameters and return type marked override.
Right. Keep going.

When a method is called through a reference of the base-class type, such as each item in a List<Vehicle>, the version that runs is chosen at run time from the actual class of the object, so a Car is charged the standard toll and a Lorry its axle-based toll. The calling code does not need an if statement to test each object's type, and a new subclass such as Coach can be added later without changing that loop. Overriding should not be confused with overloading, where several methods in the same class share a name but have different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the overloaded version from the arguments, at compile time, and no inheritance is involved.
Go on.

OOP brings three big gains: realistic modelling, productivity and maintainability. Because classes correspond to real-world entities, the design is easier to discuss with users and maps naturally onto the problem. Inheritance and class libraries mean code is written once and reused, which improves productivity, and testing effort is reduced because a superclass that has already been tested does not need retesting; only the new or overridden methods in a subclass do. Encapsulation keeps each class's data safe from accidental change, and well-defined interfaces let a team develop and test classes separately and make maintenance easier. There are disadvantages.
Makes sense. Keep going.

OOP suits some applications far better than others. It has been widely adopted for computer-aided design and manufacturing, engineering design, simulations, games and graphical interfaces, where objects are obvious, but programs that are very abstract or purely computational do not map neatly onto objects. For a small program or a straightforward data-processing job the extra design, code and memory overhead may bring little benefit. Deep hierarchies can become hard to understand, and a mistake in a base class spreads to every subclass. A good evaluation applies these points to the actual context and reaches a justified conclusion.
Go on.

In a sequential procedural program, the code decides the order in which steps happen. An event-driven program instead waits for events and responds to them, so the order of execution depends on what the user, the hardware or other software does. An event is an action or occurrence that the program can detect, such as a mouse click, a key press, a timer tick, a sensor reading or a message arriving. The program runs an event loop that listens for events and passes each one to the matching event handler, which is a subroutine attached to a particular control and event, such as btnCalculate_Click.
Got it. Keep going.

Graphical user interfaces are the best-known example. Their controls, including buttons, text boxes, labels, check boxes, list boxes and timers, are objects with properties such as Text and Enabled, methods, and events they can raise, which shows how closely gooey programming and OOP are connected. The event-driven model suits interactive software because users choose what to do next, but programmers must make sure every handler works whatever order events occur in, for example by disabling a Save button until a file is open.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Inheritance?
The mechanism by which a new, more specialised class (subclass) takes on the attributes and methods of an existing, more general class (superclass) and can add or modify its own.
Base class?
A general class whose attributes and methods are inherited by other classes.
Derived class?
A more specialised class that inherits from a base class.
Protected?
An access modifier that makes a member visible inside its own class and any subclasses but hidden from other code; shown as # in a class diagram.
Abstract class?
A class that cannot be instantiated; objects must be created from its subclasses, which must implement any abstract methods it declares.
Polymorphism?
The ability of objects of different classes to respond to the same method call in different ways.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

A complete definition of inheritance includes both ideas: a new, more specialised subclass takes on the attributes and methods (behaviours) of an existing superclass, and it can add its own or modify inherited ones. Use the terms superclass or base class and subclass or derived class correctly, and be ready to count how many attributes a subclass object has by adding inherited and new ones. For polymorphism, say that the same method call produces different behaviour for objects of different classes and support it with an example from the question, naming the overridden method. 'Evaluate' and 'discuss' questions on OOP are usually worth six marks or more and are marked in levels, so give developed points on both sides, such as more accurate modelling, reuse through inheritance and reduced testing, against unsuitability for abstract problems, extra complexity and overheads, then reach a conclusion that fits the scenario. Lists of single words earn little. When writing a subclass in C sharp, show the colon, call: base(...) in the constructor and use override where a method is replaced. For event-driven questions, use the terms event, event handler and control accurately and describe the sequence from event to output.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A Smartwatch subclass inherits three attributes from a Device superclass and adds heartRateSensor and strapSize. How many attributes does a Smartwatch object have? Is it A, 2; B, 3; C, 5; D, 6?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: 5. Attributes accumulate down the hierarchy: 3 inherited plus 2 of its own equals 5.
That's it for Inheritance, polymorphism, evaluating OOP and event-driven programming. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
